opening: What if our fear of doing the wrong thing prevents us from doing anything at all? In the Parable of the Talents, one servant buries what he has been given because he fears his master. But was his greatest mistake failing to earn more, or allowing his perception of his master to determine what he was willing to do?
prayer: Heavenly Father,  You know the gifts You have entrusted to me, the responsibilities I carry, and the fears that sometimes influence my decisions. Help me see You as the loving Father You are, not as someone waiting for me to fail. Give me the wisdom to recognize what is good, the courage to act when I should, and the humility to acknowledge when I have been wrong.  Lord Jesus, I do not want fear to prevent me from living the life You have called me to live. Teach me to use what I have been given with gratitude, generosity, and faithfulness. When I am uncertain, guide my conscience. When I am afraid, strengthen my trust. And when I become too concerned about what might go wrong, remind me of the good that may never happen if I refuse to act.  May my faith continue to grow through prayer, my love become visible through my actions, and my reverence for You lead me toward greater trust rather than fear. Above all, Lord, help me remember that You invite us not merely to fulfill our responsibilities, but to share in Your joy.  Amen.
theme: How our perception of God shapes our faith, our decisions, and our willingness to use what He has entrusted to u
body:
I have never been particularly fond of today's Gospel. The Parable of the Talents has always troubled me, perhaps because I worry that I could be like the third servant, the one who buries his master's money out of fear. But there is something else about this parable that has bothered me for years.

The third servant tells his master that he knows him to be a demanding man, someone who harvests where he has not planted and gathers where he has not scattered. To me, that sounds almost dishonest. Why would Jesus use a master who appears to profit from the work of others as an example of God? And why would the servant who refused to participate be called wicked and lazy? I have wondered whether I might have done the same thing. If I believed someone was acting dishonestly, I wouldn't want to participate either.

But as I thought more about this passage, I began to notice something I had overlooked. The master never actually tells us that he is dishonest. That is how the third servant describes him. And when the master responds, he turns the servant's own reasoning back on him. If he truly believed his master was so demanding, why hadn't he at least deposited the money in a bank where it could earn interest?

Perhaps the servant's perception of his master was the very thing preventing him from acting.

The first two servants receive different amounts of money, according to their abilities. They put what they have been given to work, and both return with more. The master praises them equally, inviting each to share in his joy. The third servant, however, does nothing. He protects what he has received, but he never allows it to become fruitful. And when he explains himself, he says something that changes how I understand the story: “Out of fear I went off and buried your talent in the ground.”

Perhaps that is what Jesus wants us to recognize. The servant was so concerned about what his master might do to him that he never discovered what he could accomplish with what had been entrusted to him.

I find this especially interesting because our perception of God can influence how we live our faith. If we see Him primarily as someone waiting to punish us for our mistakes, we may become so afraid of making the wrong decision that we hesitate to act at all. But if we know Him as a loving Father who has entrusted us with gifts and responsibilities, perhaps we become more willing to use them, even when we cannot be certain of the outcome.

Still, I struggle with something about this parable. The servants knew they had been entrusted with money, and they understood that their master would return. Our lives are not always so straightforward. We are constantly encountering situations in which no one tells us exactly what to do. We must decide whether to help, speak up, remain silent, forgive, give something away, or protect ourselves. We make these decisions according to our understanding of what is right, but what if our perception is wrong?

I think about this in my own life. I try to act thoughtfully and do what I believe is best, but I cannot always know whether I have made the right decision. Sometimes the consequences become clear only much later. Perhaps faithfulness does not mean that we will always know exactly what God wants us to do. Perhaps it means sincerely seeking what is good, using the judgment He has given us, and remaining willing to learn when we are wrong.

The first two servants were not given detailed instructions about how to invest their master's money. They had to exercise judgment and accept responsibility. And although they produced different amounts, they received the same invitation: “Come, share your master's joy.” I find comfort in that. God does not give everyone the same abilities, opportunities, or responsibilities. He knows what each of us has been given and what we are capable of doing with it. We are not being asked to live someone else's life or produce someone else's results.

Today's first reading, from Proverbs, describes a woman whose faithfulness is evident in her work, her care for her household, and her generosity toward the poor. Psalm 128 speaks of those who fear the Lord and walk in His ways. And Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, reminds us to remain awake and attentive as we await the day of the Lord. Together, these readings remind us that faith is meant to become part of how we live.

I have spent the past several days contemplating love, prayer, and the fear of not being faithful enough when Christ returns. And now this Gospel brings me back to that same question. Am I allowing my love for God to guide my decisions, or am I allowing my fear of disappointing Him to hold me back?

There is a difference between reverently fearing the Lord and living in constant fear of His rejection. I do not want to be the third servant. I do not want to bury what God has entrusted to me because I am afraid of making a mistake. But neither do I want to act recklessly, believing that any action is better than thoughtful discernment. I want to recognize the opportunities God places before me, consider them with an honest heart, and have the courage to respond.

The master tells the servants that those who have will receive more, while those who have not will lose even what they possess. At first, that seems terribly unfair. But perhaps Jesus is speaking about the fruitfulness of what we have been given. Faith grows as we live it. Love deepens as we practice it. Prayer strengthens our relationship with God as we continue returning to Him. And when we neglect these gifts, we risk allowing them to become dormant within us.

I am beginning to see that the tragedy of the third servant was not simply that he failed to earn more money. It was that his fear determined his relationship with his master and what he was willing to do.

Perhaps that is the question I need to carry with me from today's Gospel. Not whether I will always make the right decision, because I know I won't. Not whether I can accomplish as much as someone else, because that is not what God asks. But whether I trust Him enough to use what He has given me.

And when I think about the master's invitation to share in his joy, I am reminded that the purpose of our faith is not to spend our lives frightened of God. It is to grow closer to Him, to allow His gifts to bear fruit, and ultimately to share in His joy.
title: Fruit not Fear
